1992; Wilson v Coll (LO) [2011] EWHC 2824 (Admin); Bunyan v Patel [2022] EWHC 1143

DECISION 
 
1. 
The appeal was dismissed. 
 
2. 
The panel found that the appeal property should not be deleted from the council tax valuation 
list on 3 December 2020. 
 
STATEMENT OF REASONS 
 
Introduction 
 
3. 
This appeal had been brought in respect of the following: the appellant was the owner and 
council taxpayer of the property 10 Dorset House, Portland Road, Bishops Stortford, 
Hertfordshire CM23 3RU. 
 
4. 
The appellant had submitted a proposal on 4 December 2024 to delete the property from the 
council tax valuation list with effect from 3 December 2020 as it was uninhabitable due to a 
fire. 
 
5. 
The listing officer (LO) issued her decision notice on 3 November 2025 maintaining the 
property in the council tax list. 
 
6. 
The appellant appealed to the tribunal on 9 January 2026.  
 
7. 
To assist the appellant and with the agreement of the parties, the tribunal panel varied its 
model procedure and invited the LO’s representative to present his case first. 
 
8. 
This tribunal decision document is not and does not purport to be a verbatim record of 
proceedings. 
 
Relevant Law 
 
9. 
The appeal property could only be deleted from the valuation list if it had ceased to be a 
‘dwelling’. The term ‘dwelling’ is defined within Section 3(2) of the Local Government Finance 
Act 1992 as: 
 
“...any property which -  
 
(a) by virtue of the definition of hereditament in Section 115(1) of the General Rate Act 
1967, would have been a hereditament for the purposes of that Act if that Act 
remained in force; and 
(b) is not for the time being shown or required to be shown in a local or a central non-
domestic rating list in force at that time; and 
(c) is not for the time being exempt from local non-domestic rating for the purposes of 
Part III of the Local Government Finance Act 1988”    
 
10. The term ‘hereditament’ is taken from Section 115(1) of the (now repealed) General Rate Act 
1967 as: 
 
“…property which is or may become liable to a rate, being a unit of such property 
which is or would fall to be, shown as a separate item in the valuation list.”

11. A ‘dwelling’ is a unit of property which must appear as a separate entry in the valuation list if 
it is not required to appear in a non-domestic rating list or is not exempt from non-domestic 
rating. Once it has been established that a dwelling exists, it must be valued in accordance 
with the statutory assumptions contained within the Council Tax (Situation and Valuation of 
Dwellings) Regulations 1992 and, in particular, regulation 6(2)(e) “that the dwelling was in a 
reasonable state of repair”, even if the reality is very different.  
 
12. Council Tax (Alteration of Lists and Appeals) (England) Regulations 2009.  
 
13. Council Tax (Situation and Valuation of Dwellings) Regulations 1992.  
 
14. Relevant Case Law: 
 
Wilson v Coll (LO) [2011] EWHC 2824 (Admin) 
Bunyan v Patel [2022] EWHC 1143 (Admin) 
SJ & J Monk (A Firm) v Newbigin (Valuation Officer) [2017] UKSC 14 
Jackson (VO) v Canary wharf Limited [2019] UKUT 136 (LC)  
 
Issue 
15. The issue for the panel to determine was whether the appeal property should be deleted 
from the council tax list with effect from 3 December 2020 for a period of 12 months.  
 
Discussion 
 
16. The respondent had provided a consolidated evidence bundle totalling containing the 
information which had been exchanged between the parties prior to the hearing. This 
included a copy of the proposal, the appeal, the decision notice, photographs of the appeal 
property and extracts from the relevant legislation and case law. The date on which to 
consider the appeal property, the proposed effective date, was 3 December 2020.  
 
17. The appellant stated that a fire had occurred at around 10 or 11pm on Thursday 3 December 
2020 in the upstairs bedroom whilst the property was let out to tenants. The fire took hold in 
the bedroom and spread into the hall but did not go beyond, there was extensive smoke 
damage in every room in the flat and in the loft space. The Fire Service was called and put 
out the fire. 
 
18. The accommodation of the appeal property consisted of one bedroom, a bathroom, hall and 
open-plan kitchen / diner / lounge and all the surfaces and fixtures were either charred or 
smoke damaged. In the communal stairwell all the walls and ceiling were smoke affected and 
required redecoration. He had also included a copy of the Insurance payout which was 
mainly was for the loss of rent.  
 
19. In his opinion, the appeal property could not be legally occupied as it was uninhabitable for 
12 months from 3 December 2020.  
  
20. The LO’s representative stated that the property had suffered a fire and there was some 
smoke damage, however, the structure of the property remained intact and the property 
merely required repair. It was wind and watertight, there was no scheme of works being 
undertaken and the property was not truly derelict. For these reasons, the appeal property 
should remain in the list.

21. The panel noted the comments of the appellant is respect of the appeal property not being 
habitable as the damage was more than just repairs, it was extensive. However, whether a 
property is habitable or not is not the required test.  
 
22. The panel was aware that for a property to be removed from the council tax list it would need 
to have reached the state of being truly derelict, for example, if the roof or external walls were 
missing or where normal repairs would not bring it into a condition that would make it fit for 
occupation.  
 
23. The panel referred to the case of Wilson v Coll where the judge outlined the stages to follow 
when considering a dwelling in poor repair. The panel must consider if a dwelling exists. If it 
does, then the panel must assume reasonable repair. When considering whether a 
hereditament exists, the panel asked "Having regard to the character of the property and a 
reasonable amount of repair works being undertaken could the premises be occupied as a 
dwelling?".  
 
24. The panel noted that the fire report stated that the fire was confined mainly to the bedroom of 
the flat but there was no damage to any structural elements of the property. The insurance 
report referred to stripping out, cleaning, redecoration and replacement of fixtures, all of 
which the panel found constituted reasonable repair, they were not substantial and were not 
throughout all aspects of the appeal property.   
 
Decision  
 
25. The panel found that the appeal property therefore remained to be a hereditament and 
therefore a dwelling for the purposes of council tax on 3 December 2020. 
 
26. The panel therefore dismissed the appeal. 
 
Right of further appeal 
 
27. Any party who is aggrieved at the Tribunal’s decision has a statutory right of further appeal to 
the High Court on a point of law pursuant to Regulation 43 of the Tribunal Procedure 
Regulations. A party does not require permission to appeal from the Tribunal. Any appeal 
must be made directly to the High Court using Form N161 (Appellant’s Notice) within four 
weeks of the date this decision and statement of reasons was issued. 
 
28. Further information regarding this statutory right of further appeal, and the parties’ other 
rights, is contained in the guidance booklet “A guide to tribunal decisions” available on the 
Tribunal’s website at www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk/guidance-booklets/.
